title: Learning how to learn | Barbara Oakley | TEDxOaklandUniversity

segments.text: Transcriber: Tijana Mihajlović Reviewer: Mile Živković I grew up moving all over the place.
segments.vi: Người ghi âm: Tijana Mihajlović Người đánh giá: Mile Živković Tôi đã lớn lên khi di chuyển khắp nơi.

segments.text: By the time I'd hit 10th grade, I'd lived in 10 different places.
segments.vi: Đến khi tôi học lớp 10, tôi đã sống ở 10 nơi khác nhau.

segments.text: Math is extraordinarily sequential.
segments.vi: Toán học vô cùng tuần tự.

segments.text: By the time I'd hit 3rd grade, I'd fallen off the math bandwagon.
segments.vi: Khi tôi lên lớp ba, tôi đã rời khỏi xu hướng học toán.

segments.text: Basically, I flunked my way through elementary, middle, and high school math and science.
segments.vi: Về cơ bản, tôi đã trượt môn toán và khoa học ở các cấp tiểu học, trung học cơ sở và trung học phổ thông.

segments.text: So it's a little strange looking back now
segments.vi: Vì vậy, nhìn lại bây giờ có chút lạ.

segments.text: because today I am a professor of engineering and I'm passionate about my job.
segments.vi: Vì hôm nay tôi là một giáo sư kỹ thuật và tôi đam mê công việc của mình.

segments.text: One day, one of my students found out about my past,
segments.vi: Một ngày nọ, một trong những học sinh của tôi đã phát hiện ra quá khứ của tôi,

segments.text: and he asked me, "How did you do it?
segments.vi: và anh ấy hỏi tôi, “Bạn đã làm như thế nào?”

segments.text: How did you change your brain?"
segments.vi: Bạn đã thay đổi não của mình như thế nào?

segments.text: And I thought, you know, "How did I do it?"
segments.vi: Và tôi nghĩ, bạn biết đấy, “Tôi đã làm như thế nào?”

segments.text: I mean, here I was, this little kid, and I just loved language
segments.vi: Ý tôi là, tôi đây, một đứa trẻ, và tôi chỉ yêu ngôn ngữ

segments.text: and culture, and that's all I wanted to learn when I grew up,
segments.vi: và văn hoá, và đó là tất cả những gì tôi muốn học khi lớn lên,

segments.text: but I didn't have the money to go to college,
segments.vi: nhưng tôi không có tiền để đi đại học,

segments.text: so I enlisted in the army right out of high school to learn a language.
segments.vi: Vì vậy tôi đã gia nhập quân đội ngay sau khi tốt nghiệp trung học để học một ngôn ngữ.

segments.text: You can see me there, looking very nervous, about to throw a grenade.
segments.vi: Bạn có thể thấy tôi ở đó, trông rất lo lắng, sắp ném một quả lựu đạn.

segments.text: (Laughter) And I did learn a language.
segments.vi: (Cười) Và tôi đã học được một ngôn ngữ.

segments.text: I'd learned Russian, and I ended up working out on Soviet trawlers,
segments.vi: Tôi đã học tiếng Nga, và cuối cùng tôi đã làm việc trên các tàu đánh cá của Liên Xô,

segments.text: up on the Bering Sea, as a Russian translator.
segments.vi: trên biển Bering, với tư cách là một thông dịch viên tiếng Nga.

segments.text: So, I just love adventure and getting new perspectives.
segments.vi: Vì vậy, tôi chỉ yêu thích phiêu lưu và có được những góc nhìn mới.

segments.text: So I also ended up in Antarctica, at the South Pole Station.
segments.vi: Vì vậy, tôi cũng đã đến Nam Cực, tại Trạm Nam Cực.

segments.text: That's where I ended up meeting my husband.
segments.vi: Đó là nơi tôi gặp chồng mình.

segments.text: So I always say (Laughter) I had to go to the end of the Earth
segments.vi: Vì vậy, tôi luôn nói (Cười) tôi phải đi đến cùng trời cuối đất

segments.text: to meet that man.
segments.vi: gặp người đàn ông đó.

segments.text: (Laughter) But I begin to realize something, though.
segments.vi: (Cười) Nhưng tôi bắt đầu nhận ra một điều gì đó, dù sao.

segments.text: I was doing all these adventures and seeing these new perspectives,
segments.vi: Tôi đã trải qua tất cả những cuộc phiêu lưu này và nhìn thấy những góc nhìn mới.

segments.text: but somehow they were always external.
segments.vi: nhưng bằng cách nào đó chúng luôn là bên ngoài.

segments.text: They weren't internal; I wasn't changing inside.
segments.vi: Chúng không phải là nội bộ; tôi không thay đổi bên trong.

segments.text: When I'd worked in the military, I worked with all these West Point engineers,
segments.vi: Khi tôi làm việc trong quân đội, tôi đã làm việc với tất cả các kỹ sư West Point.

segments.text: and they had these powerful techniques for problem solving.
segments.vi: và họ có những kỹ thuật mạnh mẽ để giải quyết vấn đề.

segments.text: I thought, you know I'd look sometimes at what they were doing,
segments.vi: Tôi nghĩ, bạn biết đấy, đôi khi tôi sẽ xem họ đang làm gì,

segments.text: and they had these calculus and physics books, and it looked like hieroglyphics to me.
segments.vi: và họ có những cuốn sách giải tích và vật lý, và đối với tôi, chúng trông giống như chữ tượng hình.

segments.text: But I thought, "What if I could get those ideas?"
segments.vi: Nhưng tôi đã nghĩ, "Nếu tôi có thể có được những ý tưởng đó thì sao?"

segments.text: What if I could learn that language?"
segments.vi: Nếu tôi có thể học ngôn ngữ đó thì sao?

segments.text: I mean, the world's evolving.
segments.vi: Ý tôi là, thế giới đang tiến hóa.

segments.text: Language and culture are important, but math, and science, and technology are important, too.
segments.vi: Ngôn ngữ và văn hóa rất quan trọng, nhưng toán học, khoa học và công nghệ cũng quan trọng.

segments.text: What if I could learn these new ideas
segments.vi: Nếu tôi có thể học những ý tưởng mới này

segments.text: and add them to the ideas I already knew and loved?
segments.vi: và thêm chúng vào những ý tưởng mà tôi đã biết và yêu thích?

segments.text: So, when I got out of the military, at age 26,
segments.vi: Vậy, khi tôi xuất ngũ, ở tuổi 26,

segments.text: I decided to try and change my brain.
segments.vi: Tôi quyết định thử thay đổi bộ não của mình.

segments.text: It wasn't easy.
segments.vi: Không dễ dàng.

segments.text: But if I knew then what I know now about
segments.vi: Nhưng nếu tôi biết lúc đó những gì tôi biết bây giờ về

segments.text: how to learn, I could have learned much more easily and much more effectively.
segments.vi: cách học, tôi đã có thể học dễ dàng hơn và hiệu quả hơn nhiều.

segments.text: So, several years ago, as I begin trying to answer
segments.vi: Vì vậy, vài năm trước, khi tôi bắt đầu cố gắng trả lời

segments.text: that student's question, "How did I change my brain?",
segments.vi: câu hỏi của học sinh đó, "Làm thế nào tôi đã thay đổi bộ não của mình?",

segments.text: I begin reaching out to top professors from around the world,
segments.vi: Tôi bắt đầu liên hệ với các giáo sư hàng đầu từ khắp nơi trên thế giới,

segments.text: people who not only had knowledge of their difficult areas of expertise,
segments.vi: những người không chỉ có kiến thức về các lĩnh vực chuyên môn khó khăn của họ,

segments.text: but also who could teach effectively.
segments.vi: nhưng cũng ai có thể dạy hiệu quả

segments.text: And I asked them.
segments.vi: Và tôi đã hỏi họ.

segments.text: I said, "How did you learn?
segments.vi: Tôi đã nói, "Bạn đã học như thế nào?

segments.text: And how do you teach, so others could learn?"
segments.vi: Và bạn dạy như thế nào, để người khác có thể học?

segments.text: What I found was the way they learned,
segments.vi: Điều tôi tìm thấy là cách họ học,

segments.text: and the way they taught was often similar to the way I learned and I taught.
segments.vi: và cách họ dạy thường giống với cách tôi học và tôi đã dạy.

segments.text: It was almost like this kind of shared fraternal handshake.
segments.vi: Nó gần giống như một cái bắt tay huynh đệ chia sẻ như thế này.

segments.text: But we often didn't know why we did what we did.
segments.vi: Nhưng chúng ta thường không biết tại sao mình lại làm những gì mình đã làm.

segments.text: So I begin researching neuroscience and cognitive psychology,
segments.vi: Vì vậy, tôi bắt đầu nghiên cứu khoa học thần kinh và tâm lý học nhận thức,

segments.text: and reaching out to talk to top experts of those fields.
segments.vi: và tiếp cận để nói chuyện với các chuyên gia hàng đầu trong những lĩnh vực đó.

segments.text: Here is what I found, the keys to learning effectively.
As we know, the brain is enormously complex.
But we can simplify its operation into two fundamentally different modes.
The first is just what I'll call the focus mode.
The focus mode is just like it sounds like:
you turn your attention to something and boom! It's on.
But the second mode is a little different.
It's a relaxed set of neural states that I'll call the diffuse mode.
It's a number of resting states.
So it seems that, when you're learning, you're going back
and forth between these two different modes.
How can we better understand these modes? Through analogy.
What we're going to use is a pinball machine analogy.
You all know how pinballs work.
You just pull back on a plunger, and the ball goes boinking out
and bounces around on the rubber bumpers, and that's how you get points.
What we're going to do is we're going to take this pinball
and we're going to put it right on your brain.
So, there it is.
There's the pinball machine on your brain.
If you look, this is the analogy for the focus mode.
When you're learning, you're often thinking tightly, as you're focusing on something.
It involves thoughts you're somewhat familiar with, perhaps historical patterns,
or you're familiar with the multiplication table.
So you think a thought, and it takes off,
and moves along smoothly, pretty much along the pathways that you've already laid.
But what if the thought you're thinking is actually a new thought,
a new concept, a new technique that you've never thought of before?
Well, that's symbolized by this new pattern towards the bottom of the pinball machine metaphor.
To get to this new place, I mean,
at least sort of metaphorically speaking, look at all the rubber bumpers
that are in the way.
How can you even get there?
You need a different way of thinking, a new perspective in a sense,
and that's provided here by the diffuse mode.
Look at how far apart those rubber bumpers are from one another.
When you think a thought, it takes off,
and it can range very widely, as you're attempting to come up with some new ideas.
So, you can't do that careful, focused thinking
that you can in the focus mode, but you can,
at least, get to the place you need to be in to grapple
with these new ideas.
The bottom line for all of us out
of this is this: when you're learning, you want to go back
and forth between these modes, and if you find yourself,
as you're focusing in on something, trying to learn a new concept
or solve a problem, and you get stuck,
you want to turn your attention away from that problem
and allow the diffuse modes, those resting states, to do their work in the background.
How can we actually use these ideas in real life?
If you look at this guy right here, he was Salvador Dali,
one of the most brilliant surrealist painters of the 20th century.
Dali was the very definition of a wild and crazy guy.
You can see him there.
He's got his pet, Ocelot Babu.
What Dali used to do when he was kind of stuck
as he was solving some problem related to his painting was he'd sit down
and he'd relax in a chair, and he'd have keys in his hands.
He'd hold those keys, and he'd relax, kind of letting his brain noodling away.
Just as he'd relax so much that he'd fall asleep,
the keys would fall from his hands, the clatter would wake him up,
and off you go:
he'd take those ideas from the diffuse mode over to the focus mode,
where he could work with them, refine them, and use them for his painting.
You might think, "That's great!
It's good for an artist.
But I'm an engineer.
So how can I use these ideas?"
If you see this guy right here, he was Thomas Edison,
one of the most brilliant inventors in history.
What Edison used to like to do, at least according to legend,
he'd sit in a chair with ball bearings in his hand.
He'd relax away, kind of thinking about the problem, loosely,
that he was trying to solve related to his inventions, relaxing.
Just as he'd fall asleep, the ball bearings would fall from his hands,
and off you go: he'd be woken up,
and he'd take those ideas from the diffuse mode back into the focus mode.
He'd use them to refine and finish his inventions.
The bottom line for all of us out
of this is this: whenever you're sitting down to solve a new problem
or analyze a new idea, even if millions of other people have thought the same thoughts,
or solved the same problems, for you, it's just as creative
as it was for famous people like Dali and Edison,
and you want to use some of these creative approaches.
But you might say to me, "Yeah, but I've got a problem, though.
You know, I just love to procrastinate.
This back and forth stuff is great, but I don't have time.
I cram at the last minute.
That's just me."
So, let's talk just a little bit about procrastination.
What seems to happen when you procrastinate
is this: you look at something you'd really rather not do,
and you actually feel a physical pain in the part of your brain that analyzes pain.
So, there are two ways that you can handle this.
The first way is you can just kind of keep working a way through it.
And research has shown that within a few minutes it actually will disappear.
But the second way is you just turn your attention away, and guess what?
You feel better, right, right away.
(Laughter) So, you do this once, you do this twice;
it's just not that big a deal.
But you do this very often, and it's actually like an addiction.
It can really cause problems in how you lead your life.
So, how can you handle it?
A very simple way: using the Pomodoro Technique.
The Pomodoro technique, as it turns out,
all you need to do is you get a timer.
Any timer will do.
Then you just take it and set it for 25 minutes,
and make sure everything else is turned off so, no instant messengers,
